<div sID="gen24484" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Mark.5" sID="Mark.5"/> <div eID="gen24484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24485" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24486" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, we have, I. Christ's casting the legion of devils out of the man possessed, and suffering them to enter into the swine, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.1-Mark.5.20">ver. 1-20</reference>. II. Christ's healing the woman with the bloody issue, in the way as he was going to raise Jairus's daughter to life, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.21-Mark.5.43">ver. 21-43</reference>. These three miracles we had the story of before (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.28">Matt. viii. 28,</reference> and <reference osisRef="Matt.9.18">Matt. ix. 18</reference>, and c.) but more fully related here.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen24486" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24485" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Expulsion of Legion.</title> <div sID="gen24487" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And they came over unto the other side of the sea, into the country of the Gadarenes. <hi type="super">2</hi> And when he was come out of the ship, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit, <hi type="super">3</hi> Who had <hi type="italic">his</hi> dwelling among the tombs; and no man could bind him, no, not with chains: 4 Because that he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken in pieces: neither could any <hi type="italic">man</hi> tame him. 5 And always, night and day, he was in the mountains, and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones. <hi type="super">6</hi> But when he saw Jesus afar off, he ran and worshipped him, <hi type="super">7</hi> And cried with a loud voice, and said, What have I to do with thee, Jesus, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> Son of the most high God? I adjure thee by God, that thou torment me not. <hi type="super">8</hi> For he said unto him, Come out of the man, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> unclean spirit. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he asked him, What <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy name? And he answered, saying, My name <hi type="italic">is</hi> Legion: for we are many. <hi type="super">10</hi> And he besought him much that he would not send them away out of the country. <hi type="super">11</hi> Now there was there nigh unto the mountains a great herd of swine feeding. 12 And all the devils besought him, saying, Send us into the swine, that we may enter into them. <hi type="super">13</hi> And forthwith Jesus gave them leave. And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea. 14 And they that fed the swine fled, and told <hi type="italic">it</hi> in the city, and in the country. And they went out to see what it was that was done. <hi type="super">15</hi> And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid. <hi type="super">16</hi> And they that saw <hi type="italic">it</hi> told them how it befell to him that was possessed with the devil, and <hi type="italic">also</hi> concerning the swine. 17 And they began to pray him to depart out of their coasts. 18 And when he was come into the ship, he that had been possessed with the devil prayed him that he might be with him. 19 Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee. <hi type="super">20</hi> And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all <hi type="italic">men</hi> did marvel. <div eID="gen24487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24488" type="x-p"/> We have here an instance of Christ's dispossessing the strong man armed, and disposing of him as he pleased, to make it appear that he was <hi type="italic">stronger than he.</hi> This he did when he was come <hi type="italic">to the other side,</hi> whither he went through a storm; his business there was to rescue this poor creature out of the hands of Satan, and when he had done that, he returned. Thus he came from heaven to earth, and returned, in a storm, to redeem a remnant of mankind out of the hands of the devil, though but a <hi type="italic">little remnant,</hi> and did not think his pains <hi type="italic">ill bestowed.</hi> <div eID="gen24488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24489" type="x-p"/> In Matthew, they were said to be <hi type="italic">two</hi> possessed with devils; here it is said to be a <hi type="italic">man</hi> possessed with an unclean spirit. If there were <hi type="italic">two,</hi> there was one, and Mark doth not say that there was <hi type="italic">but one;</hi> so that this difference cannot give us any just offence; it is probable that one of them was much more remarkable than the other, and said what was said. Now observe here, <div eID="gen24489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24490" type="x-p"/> I. The miserable condition that this poor creature was in; he was under the power of an <hi type="italic">unclean spirit,</hi> the devil got possession of him, and the effect of it was not, as in many, a silent melancholy, but a raging frenzy; he was raving mad; his condition seems to have been worse than any of the possessed, that were Christ's patients. <div eID="gen24490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24491" type="x-p"/> 1. He had <hi type="italic">his dwelling among the tombs,</hi> among the graves of dead people. Their tombs were out of the cities, in <hi type="italic">desolate places</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.3.14">Job iii. 14</reference>); which gave the devil great advantage: for <hi type="italic">woe to him that is alone.</hi> Perhaps the devil drove him to <hi type="italic">the tombs,</hi> to make people fancy that the souls of the dead were turned into dæmons, and did what mischief was done, so to excuse themselves from it. The touch of a grave was polluting, <reference osisRef="Num.19.16">Num. xix. 16</reference>. The <hi type="italic">unclean spirit</hi> drives people into that company that is <hi type="italic">defiling,</hi> and so keeps possession of them. Christ, by rescuing souls out of Satan's power, <hi type="italic">saves the living from among the dead.</hi> <div eID="gen24491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24492" type="x-p"/> 2. He was very strong and ungovernable; <hi type="italic">No man could bind him,</hi> as it is requisite both for their own good, and for the safety of others, that those who are distracted should be. Not only cords would not hold him, but <hi type="italic">chains</hi> and <hi type="italic">fetters of iron</hi> would not, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.3-Mark.5.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. Very deplorable is the case of such as <hi type="italic">need to be</hi> thus <hi type="italic">bound,</hi> and of all miserable people in this world they are most to be pitied; but his case was worst of all, in whom the devil was so strong, that he could not be <hi type="italic">bound.</hi> This sets forth the sad condition of those souls in which the devil has dominion; those <hi type="italic">children of disobedience,</hi> in whom that unclean spirit works. Some notoriously wilful sinners are like this madman; all are herein <hi type="italic">like the horse and the mule,</hi> that they need to be <hi type="italic">held in with bit and bridle;</hi> but some are like the <hi type="italic">wild ass,</hi> that will not be so held. The commands and curses of the law are as <hi type="italic">chains</hi> and <hi type="italic">fetters,</hi> to restrain sinners from their wicked courses; but they <hi type="italic">break those bands in sunder,</hi> and it is an evidence of the power of the devil in them. <div eID="gen24492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24493" type="x-p"/> 3. He was a terror and torment to himself and to all about him, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.5">v. 5</reference>. The devil is a <hi type="italic">cruel</hi> master to those that are <hi type="italic">led captive</hi> by him, a perfect tyrant; this wretched creature was <hi type="italic">night and day in the mountains and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones,</hi> either bemoaning his own deplorable case, or in a rage and indignation against heaven. Men in frenzies often wound and destroy themselves; what is a man, when reason is <hi type="italic">de</hi>throned and Satan <hi type="italic">en</hi>throned? The worshippers of Baal in their fury <hi type="italic">cut themselves,</hi> like this madman in his. The voice of God is, <hi type="italic">Do thyself no harm;</hi> the voice of Satan is, <hi type="italic">Do thyself all the harm thou canst;</hi> yet God's word is despised, and Satan's regarded. Perhaps his <hi type="italic">cutting himself with stones</hi> was only cutting his feet with the sharp stones he ran barefoot upon. <div eID="gen24493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24494" type="x-p"/> II. His application to Christ (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.6">v. 6</reference>); <hi type="italic">When he saw Jesus afar off,</hi> coming ashore, he <hi type="italic">ran, and worshipped him.</hi> He usually <hi type="italic">ran upon</hi> others with <hi type="italic">rage,</hi> but he <hi type="italic">ran to</hi> Christ with <hi type="italic">reverence.</hi> That was done by an invisible hand of Christ, which could not be done with chains and fetters; his fury was all on a sudden curbed. Even the devil, in this poor creature, was forced to tremble before Christ, and bow to him: or, rather, the poor man came, and <hi type="italic">worshipped Christ,</hi> in a sense of the need he had of his help, the power of Satan in and over him being, for this instant, suspended. <div eID="gen24494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24495" type="x-p"/> III. The word of command Christ gave to the unclean spirit, to quit his possession (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.8">v. 8</reference>); <hi type="italic">Come out of him, thou unclean spirit.</hi> He made the man desirous to be relieved, when he enabled him to <hi type="italic">run, and worship him,</hi> and then put forth his power for his relief. If Christ <hi type="italic">work in us</hi> heartily to pray for a deliverance from Satan, he will work for us that deliverance. Here is an instance of the power and authority with which Christ <hi type="italic">commanded the unclean spirits, and they obeyed him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.1.27">ch. i. 27</reference>. He said, <hi type="italic">Come out of the man.</hi> The design of Christ's gospel is to <hi type="italic">expel</hi> unclean spirits out of the souls of people; "<hi type="italic">Come out of the man, thou unclean spirit,</hi> that the Holy Spirit may enter, may take possession of the heart, and have dominion in it." <div eID="gen24495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24496" type="x-p"/> IV. The dread which the devil had of Christ. The <hi type="italic">man ran,</hi> and <hi type="italic">worshipped Christ;</hi> but it was the devil in the man, that <hi type="italic">cried with a loud voice</hi> (making use of the poor man's tongue), <hi type="italic">What have I to do with thee?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.7">v. 7</reference>. Just as that other unclean spirit, <reference osisRef="Mark.1.24">ch. i. 24</reference>. 1. He calls God the <hi type="italic">most high God,</hi> above all other gods. By the name <hi type="italic">Elion—the Most High,</hi> God was <hi type="italic">known</hi> among the Ph&#339;nicians, and the other nations that bordered upon Israel; and by that name the devil calls him. 2. He owns Jesus to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God.</hi> Note, It is no strange thing to hear the best words drop from the worst mouths. There is such a way of saying this as none can attain to but <hi type="italic">by the Holy Ghost</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.3">1 Cor. xii. 3</reference>); yet it may be said, after a sort, by the <hi type="italic">unclean spirit.</hi> There is no judging of men by their loose sayings; but by their fruits ye shall know them. Piety from the teeth outward is an easy thing. The most fair-spoken hypocrite cannot say better than to call Jesus the Son of God, and yet that the devil did. 3. He disowns any design against Christ; "<hi type="italic">What have I to do with thee?</hi> I have no need of thee, I pretend to none; I desire to have nothing to do with thee; I <hi type="italic">cannot stand</hi> before thee, and <hi type="italic">would not</hi> fall." 4. He deprecates his wrath; I <hi type="italic">adjure thee,</hi> that is, "I earnestly beseech thee, by all that is sacred, I beg of thee for God's sake, by whose permission I have got possession of this man, that, though thou drive me out hence, yet that thou <hi type="italic">torment me not,</hi> that thou do not restrain me from doing mischief somewhere else; though I know I am <hi type="italic">sentenced,</hi> yet let me not be <hi type="italic">sent</hi> to the chains of darkness, or hindered from going to and fro, to <hi type="italic">devour.</hi>" <div eID="gen24496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24497" type="x-p"/> V. The account Christ took from this unclean spirit of his name. This we had not in Matthew. Christ asked him, <hi type="italic">What is thy name?</hi> Not but that Christ could call all the <hi type="italic">fallen</hi> stars, as well as the <hi type="italic">morning</hi> stars, by their names; but he demands this, that the standers by might be affected with the vast numbers and power of those malignant infernal spirits, as they had reason to be, when the answer was, <hi type="italic">My name is Legion, for we are many;</hi> a <hi type="italic">legion</hi> of soldiers among the Romans consisted, some say, of six thousand men, others of twelve thousand and five hundred; but the number of a legion with them, like that of a regiment with us, was not always the same. Now this intimates that the devils, the infernal powers, are, 1. <hi type="italic">Military</hi> powers; a legion is a number of soldiers in arms. The devils war against God and his glory, Christ and his gospel, men and their holiness and happiness. They are such as we are to <hi type="italic">resist</hi> and <hi type="italic">wrestle against,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Eph. vi. 12</reference>. 2. That they are <hi type="italic">numerous;</hi> he <hi type="italic">owns,</hi> or rather he <hi type="italic">boasts—We are many;</hi> as if he hoped to be <hi type="italic">too many</hi> for Christ himself to deal with. What multitudes of apostate spirits were there, and all enemies to God and man; when here were a legion posted to keep garrison in one poor wretched creature against Christ! Many there are that rise up against us. 3. That they are <hi type="italic">unanimous;</hi> they are <hi type="italic">many</hi> devils, and yet but <hi type="italic">one legion</hi> engaged in the same wicked cause; and therefore that cavil of the Pharisees, which supposed Satan to cast out Satan, and to be divided against himself, was altogether groundless. It was not <hi type="italic">one</hi> of this legion that betrayed the rest, for they all said, as one man, <hi type="italic">What have I to do with thee?</hi> 4. That they are very <hi type="italic">powerful;</hi> Who can stand before a <hi type="italic">legion?</hi> We are not a match for our spiritual enemies, in our own strength; but <hi type="italic">in the Lord, and in the power of his might,</hi> we shall be able to <hi type="italic">stand against them,</hi> though there are legions of them. 5. That there is <hi type="italic">order</hi> among them, as there is in a <hi type="italic">legion;</hi> there are <hi type="italic">principalities, and powers, and rulers of the darkness of this world,</hi> which supposes that there are those of a lower rank; the <hi type="italic">devil</hi> and his angels; the <hi type="italic">dragon</hi> and his; the prince of the devils and his subjects: which makes those enemies the more formidable. <div eID="gen24497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24498" type="x-p"/> VI. The request of this legion, that Christ would suffer them to go into a herd of swine that was <hi type="italic">feeding nigh unto the mountains</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.11">v. 11</reference>), those mountains which the demoniacs haunted, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.5">v. 5</reference>. Their request was, 1. That he <hi type="italic">would not send them away out of the country</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.10">v. 10</reference>); not only that he would not <hi type="italic">commit</hi> them, or <hi type="italic">confine</hi> them, to their infernal prison, and so <hi type="italic">torment them before the time;</hi> but that he would not <hi type="italic">banish</hi> them <hi type="italic">that country,</hi> as justly he might, because in this poor man they had been such a terror to it, and done so much mischief. They seem to have had a particular affection for <hi type="italic">that country;</hi> or, rather, a particular spite to it; and to have liberty to walk <hi type="italic">to and fro through</hi> the rest of <hi type="italic">the earth,</hi> will not serve (<reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job i. 7</reference>), unless the <hi type="italic">range of those mountains</hi> be allowed them for their pasture, <reference osisRef="Job.39.8">Job xxxix. 8</reference>. But why would they abide in <hi type="italic">that country?</hi> Grotius saith, Because in <hi type="italic">that country</hi> there were many <hi type="italic">apostate Jews,</hi> who had thrown themselves out of the covenant of God, and had thereby given Satan power over them. And some suggest, that, having by experience got the knowledge of the dispositions and manners of the people of that country, they could the more effectually do them mischief by their temptations. 2. That he would suffer them to <hi type="italic">enter into the swine,</hi> by destroying which they hoped to do more mischief to the souls of all the people in the country, than they could by entering into the body of any particular person, which therefore they did not ask leave to do, for they knew Christ would not grant it. <div eID="gen24498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24499" type="x-p"/> VII. The permission Christ gave them to enter into the swine, and the immediate destruction of the swine thereby; <hi type="italic">He gave them leave</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.13">v. 13</reference>), he did not forbid or restrain them, he let them do as they had a mind. Thus he would let the Gadarenes see what powerful spiteful enemies devils are, that they might thereby be induced to make him their Friend, who alone was able to control and conquer them, and had made it appear that he was so. Immediately the <hi type="italic">unclean spirits entered into the swine,</hi> which by the law were unclean creatures, and naturally love to <hi type="italic">wallow in the mire,</hi> the fittest place for them. Those that, like the swine, delight in <hi type="italic">the mire</hi> of sensual lusts, are fit habitations for Satan, and are, like Babylon, the <hi type="italic">hold of every foul spirit,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">cage of every unclean and hateful bird</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.18.2">Rev. xviii. 2</reference>), as pure souls are habitations of the Holy Spirit. The consequence of the devils entering into the swine, was, that they all <hi type="italic">ran mad</hi> presently, and ran headlong into the adjoining sea, where they were all drowned, to the number of <hi type="italic">two thousand.</hi> The man they possessed did only <hi type="italic">cut himself,</hi> for God had said, <hi type="italic">He is in your hands, only save his life.</hi> But thereby it appeared, that, if he had not been so restrained, the poor man would have <hi type="italic">drowned himself.</hi> See how much we are indebted to the providence of God, and the ministration of good angels, for our preservation from malignant spirits. <div eID="gen24499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24500" type="x-p"/> VIII. The report of all this dispersed through the country immediately. They that <hi type="italic">fed the swine,</hi> hastened to the owners, to give an account of their charge, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.14">v. 14</reference>. This drew the people together, to see what was done: and, 1. When they saw how wonderfully the poor man was cured, they hence conceived a <hi type="italic">veneration for Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.15">v. 15</reference>. They saw him that was <hi type="italic">possessed with the devil,</hi> and knew him well enough, by the same token that they had many a time been frightened at the sight of him; and were now as much surprised to see him <hi type="italic">sitting clothed and in his right mind;</hi> when Satan was cast out, he came to himself, and was his own man presently. Note, Those who are grave and sober, and live by rule and with consideration, thereby make it appear that by the power of Christ the devil's power is broken in their souls. The sight of this <hi type="italic">made them afraid;</hi> it astonished them, and forced them to own the power of Christ, and that he is <hi type="italic">worthy to be feared.</hi> But, 2. When they found that their swine were lost, they thence conceived a <hi type="italic">dislike of Christ,</hi> and wished to have rather his room than his company; they prayed him to <hi type="italic">depart out of their coasts,</hi> for they think not any good he can do them sufficient to make them amends for the loss of so many swine, fat swine, it may be, and ready for the market. Now the devils had what they would have; for by no handle do these evil spirits more effectually manage sinful souls than by that of the love of the world. They were afraid of some further punishment, if Christ should tarry among them, whereas, if they would but part with their sins, he had life and happiness for them; but, being loth to quit either their sins or their swine, they chose rather to abandon their Saviour. Thus <hi type="italic">they</hi> do, who, rather than let go a base lust, will throw away their interest in Christ, and their expectations from him. They should rather have argued, "If he has such a power as this over devils and all creatures, it is good having him our Friend; if the devils have leave to tarry <hi type="italic">in our country</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.10">v. 10</reference>), let us entreat <hi type="italic">him</hi> to tarry in it too, who alone can control them." But, instead of this, they wished him further off. Such strange misconstructions do carnal hearts make of the just judgments of God; instead of being by them driven to him as they ought, they set him at so much the greater distance; though he hath said, <hi type="italic">Provoke me not, and I will do you no hurt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.25.6">Jer. xxv. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen24500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24501" type="x-p"/> IX. An account of the conduct of the poor man after his deliverance. 1. He <hi type="italic">desired that he might go along with Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.18">v. 18</reference>), perhaps for fear lest the evil spirit should again seize him; or, rather, that he might receive instruction from him, being unwilling to stay among those heathenish people that desired him to depart. Those that are freed from the evil spirit, cannot but covet acquaintance and fellowship with Christ. 2. Christ <hi type="italic">would not suffer him</hi> to go with him, lest it should savour of ostentation, and to let him know that he could both protect and instruct him at a distance. And besides, he had other work for him to do; he must go home to his friends, and tell them what <hi type="italic">great things the Lord had done for him,</hi> the Lord Jesus had done; that Christ might be honoured, and his neighbours and friends might be edified, and invited to believe in Christ. He must take particular notice rather of Christ's <hi type="italic">pity</hi> than of his <hi type="italic">power,</hi> for that is it which especially he glories in; he must tell them what <hi type="italic">compassion</hi> the Lord had had on him in his misery. 3. The man, in a transport of joy, proclaimed, all the country over, what <hi type="italic">great things Jesus had done for him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.20">v. 20</reference>. This is a debt we owe both to Christ and to our brethren, that he may be glorified and they edified. And see what was the effect of it; <hi type="italic">All men did marvel,</hi> but few went any further. Many that cannot but wonder at the works of Christ, yet do not, as they ought, <hi type="italic">wonder after him.</hi>
entries.content_plain: The Expulsion of Legion. 1 And they came over unto the other side of the sea, into the country of the Gadarenes. 2 And when he was come out of the ship, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit, 3 Who had his dwelling among the tombs; and no man could bind him, no, not with chains: 4 Because that he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken in pieces: neither could any man tame him. 5 And always, night and day, he was in the mountains, and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones. 6 But when he saw Jesus afar off, he ran and worshipped him, 7 And cried with a loud voice, and said, What have I to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of the most high God? I adjure thee by God, that thou torment me not. 8 For he said unto him, Come out of the man, thou unclean spirit. 9 And he asked him, What is thy name? And he answered, saying, My name is Legion: for we are many. 10 And he besought him much that he would not send them away out of the country. 11 Now there was there nigh unto the mountains a great herd of swine feeding. 12 And all the devils besought him, saying, Send us into the swine, that we may enter into them. 13 And forthwith Jesus gave them leave. And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea. 14 And they that fed the swine fled, and told it in the city, and in the country. And they went out to see what it was that was done. 15 And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid. 16 And they that saw it told them how it befell to him that was possessed with the devil, and also concerning the swine. 17 And they began to pray him to depart out of their coasts. 18 And when he was come into the ship, he that had been possessed with the devil prayed him that he might be with him. 19 Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee. 20 And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all men did marvel. We have here an instance of Christ's dispossessing the strong man armed, and disposing of him as he pleased, to make it appear that he was stronger than he. This he did when he was come to the other side, whither he went through a storm; his business there was to rescue this poor creature out of the hands of Satan, and when he had done that, he returned. Thus he came from heaven to earth, and returned, in a storm, to redeem a remnant of mankind out of the hands of the devil, though but a little remnant, and did not think his pains ill bestowed. In Matthew, they were said to be two possessed with devils; here it is said to be a man possessed with an unclean spirit. If there were two, there was one, and Mark doth not say that there was but one; so that this difference cannot give us any just offence; it is probable that one of them was much more remarkable than the other, and said what was said. Now observe here, I. This is a debt we owe both to Christ and to our brethren, that he may be glorified and they edified. And see what was the effect of it; All men did marvel, but few went any further. Many that cannot but wonder at the works of Christ, yet do not, as they ought, wonder after him.
entries.reader_content_osis: <hi type="super">1</hi> And they came over unto the other side of the sea, into the country of the Gadarenes. <hi type="super">2</hi> And when he was come out of the ship, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit, <hi type="super">3</hi> Who had <hi type="italic">his</hi> dwelling among the tombs; and no man could bind him, no, not with chains: 4 Because that he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken in pieces: neither could any <hi type="italic">man</hi> tame him. 5 And always, night and day, he was in the mountains, and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones. <hi type="super">6</hi> But when he saw Jesus afar off, he ran and worshipped him, <hi type="super">7</hi> And cried with a loud voice, and said, What have I to do with thee, Jesus, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> Son of the most high God? I adjure thee by God, that thou torment me not. <hi type="super">8</hi> For he said unto him, Come out of the man, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> unclean spirit. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he asked him, What <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy name? And he answered, saying, My name <hi type="italic">is</hi> Legion: for we are many. <hi type="super">10</hi> And he besought him much that he would not send them away out of the country. <hi type="super">11</hi> Now there was there nigh unto the mountains a great herd of swine feeding. 12 And all the devils besought him, saying, Send us into the swine, that we may enter into them. <hi type="super">13</hi> And forthwith Jesus gave them leave. And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea. 14 And they that fed the swine fled, and told <hi type="italic">it</hi> in the city, and in the country. And they went out to see what it was that was done. <hi type="super">15</hi> And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid. <hi type="super">16</hi> And they that saw <hi type="italic">it</hi> told them how it befell to him that was possessed with the devil, and <hi type="italic">also</hi> concerning the swine. 17 And they began to pray him to depart out of their coasts. 18 And when he was come into the ship, he that had been possessed with the devil prayed him that he might be with him. 19 Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee. <hi type="super">20</hi> And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all <hi type="italic">men</hi> did marvel. <div eID="gen24487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24488" type="x-p"/> We have here an instance of Christ's dispossessing the strong man armed, and disposing of him as he pleased, to make it appear that he was <hi type="italic">stronger than he.</hi> This he did when he was come <hi type="italic">to the other side,</hi> whither he went through a storm; his business there was to rescue this poor creature out of the hands of Satan, and when he had done that, he returned. Thus he came from heaven to earth, and returned, in a storm, to redeem a remnant of mankind out of the hands of the devil, though but a <hi type="italic">little remnant,</hi> and did not think his pains <hi type="italic">ill bestowed.</hi> <div eID="gen24488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24489" type="x-p"/> In Matthew, they were said to be <hi type="italic">two</hi> possessed with devils; here it is said to be a <hi type="italic">man</hi> possessed with an unclean spirit. If there were <hi type="italic">two,</hi> there was one, and Mark doth not say that there was <hi type="italic">but one;</hi> so that this difference cannot give us any just offence; it is probable that one of them was much more remarkable than the other, and said what was said. Now observe here, <div eID="gen24489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24490" type="x-p"/> I. The miserable condition that this poor creature was in; he was under the power of an <hi type="italic">unclean spirit,</hi> the devil got possession of him, and the effect of it was not, as in many, a silent melancholy, but a raging frenzy; he was raving mad; his condition seems to have been worse than any of the possessed, that were Christ's patients. <div eID="gen24490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24491" type="x-p"/> 1. He had <hi type="italic">his dwelling among the tombs,</hi> among the graves of dead people. Their tombs were out of the cities, in <hi type="italic">desolate places</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.3.14">Job iii. 14</reference>); which gave the devil great advantage: for <hi type="italic">woe to him that is alone.</hi> Perhaps the devil drove him to <hi type="italic">the tombs,</hi> to make people fancy that the souls of the dead were turned into dæmons, and did what mischief was done, so to excuse themselves from it. The touch of a grave was polluting, <reference osisRef="Num.19.16">Num. xix. 16</reference>. The <hi type="italic">unclean spirit</hi> drives people into that company that is <hi type="italic">defiling,</hi> and so keeps possession of them. Christ, by rescuing souls out of Satan's power, <hi type="italic">saves the living from among the dead.</hi> <div eID="gen24491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24492" type="x-p"/> 2. He was very strong and ungovernable; <hi type="italic">No man could bind him,</hi> as it is requisite both for their own good, and for the safety of others, that those who are distracted should be. Not only cords would not hold him, but <hi type="italic">chains</hi> and <hi type="italic">fetters of iron</hi> would not, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.3-Mark.5.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. Very deplorable is the case of such as <hi type="italic">need to be</hi> thus <hi type="italic">bound,</hi> and of all miserable people in this world they are most to be pitied; but his case was worst of all, in whom the devil was so strong, that he could not be <hi type="italic">bound.</hi> This sets forth the sad condition of those souls in which the devil has dominion; those <hi type="italic">children of disobedience,</hi> in whom that unclean spirit works. Some notoriously wilful sinners are like this madman; all are herein <hi type="italic">like the horse and the mule,</hi> that they need to be <hi type="italic">held in with bit and bridle;</hi> but some are like the <hi type="italic">wild ass,</hi> that will not be so held. The commands and curses of the law are as <hi type="italic">chains</hi> and <hi type="italic">fetters,</hi> to restrain sinners from their wicked courses; but they <hi type="italic">break those bands in sunder,</hi> and it is an evidence of the power of the devil in them. <div eID="gen24492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24493" type="x-p"/> 3. He was a terror and torment to himself and to all about him, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.5">v. 5</reference>. The devil is a <hi type="italic">cruel</hi> master to those that are <hi type="italic">led captive</hi> by him, a perfect tyrant; this wretched creature was <hi type="italic">night and day in the mountains and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones,</hi> either bemoaning his own deplorable case, or in a rage and indignation against heaven. Men in frenzies often wound and destroy themselves; what is a man, when reason is <hi type="italic">de</hi>throned and Satan <hi type="italic">en</hi>throned? The worshippers of Baal in their fury <hi type="italic">cut themselves,</hi> like this madman in his. The voice of God is, <hi type="italic">Do thyself no harm;</hi> the voice of Satan is, <hi type="italic">Do thyself all the harm thou canst;</hi> yet God's word is despised, and Satan's regarded. Perhaps his <hi type="italic">cutting himself with stones</hi> was only cutting his feet with the sharp stones he ran barefoot upon. <div eID="gen24493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24494" type="x-p"/> II. His application to Christ (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.6">v. 6</reference>); <hi type="italic">When he saw Jesus afar off,</hi> coming ashore, he <hi type="italic">ran, and worshipped him.</hi> He usually <hi type="italic">ran upon</hi> others with <hi type="italic">rage,</hi> but he <hi type="italic">ran to</hi> Christ with <hi type="italic">reverence.</hi> That was done by an invisible hand of Christ, which could not be done with chains and fetters; his fury was all on a sudden curbed. Even the devil, in this poor creature, was forced to tremble before Christ, and bow to him: or, rather, the poor man came, and <hi type="italic">worshipped Christ,</hi> in a sense of the need he had of his help, the power of Satan in and over him being, for this instant, suspended. <div eID="gen24494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24495" type="x-p"/> III. The word of command Christ gave to the unclean spirit, to quit his possession (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.8">v. 8</reference>); <hi type="italic">Come out of him, thou unclean spirit.</hi> He made the man desirous to be relieved, when he enabled him to <hi type="italic">run, and worship him,</hi> and then put forth his power for his relief. If Christ <hi type="italic">work in us</hi> heartily to pray for a deliverance from Satan, he will work for us that deliverance. Here is an instance of the power and authority with which Christ <hi type="italic">commanded the unclean spirits, and they obeyed him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.1.27">ch. i. 27</reference>. He said, <hi type="italic">Come out of the man.</hi> The design of Christ's gospel is to <hi type="italic">expel</hi> unclean spirits out of the souls of people; "<hi type="italic">Come out of the man, thou unclean spirit,</hi> that the Holy Spirit may enter, may take possession of the heart, and have dominion in it." <div eID="gen24495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24496" type="x-p"/> IV. The dread which the devil had of Christ. The <hi type="italic">man ran,</hi> and <hi type="italic">worshipped Christ;</hi> but it was the devil in the man, that <hi type="italic">cried with a loud voice</hi> (making use of the poor man's tongue), <hi type="italic">What have I to do with thee?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.7">v. 7</reference>. Just as that other unclean spirit, <reference osisRef="Mark.1.24">ch. i. 24</reference>. 1. He calls God the <hi type="italic">most high God,</hi> above all other gods. By the name <hi type="italic">Elion—the Most High,</hi> God was <hi type="italic">known</hi> among the Ph&#339;nicians, and the other nations that bordered upon Israel; and by that name the devil calls him. 2. He owns Jesus to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God.</hi> Note, It is no strange thing to hear the best words drop from the worst mouths. There is such a way of saying this as none can attain to but <hi type="italic">by the Holy Ghost</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.3">1 Cor. xii. 3</reference>); yet it may be said, after a sort, by the <hi type="italic">unclean spirit.</hi> There is no judging of men by their loose sayings; but by their fruits ye shall know them. Piety from the teeth outward is an easy thing. The most fair-spoken hypocrite cannot say better than to call Jesus the Son of God, and yet that the devil did. 3. He disowns any design against Christ; "<hi type="italic">What have I to do with thee?</hi> I have no need of thee, I pretend to none; I desire to have nothing to do with thee; I <hi type="italic">cannot stand</hi> before thee, and <hi type="italic">would not</hi> fall." 4. He deprecates his wrath; I <hi type="italic">adjure thee,</hi> that is, "I earnestly beseech thee, by all that is sacred, I beg of thee for God's sake, by whose permission I have got possession of this man, that, though thou drive me out hence, yet that thou <hi type="italic">torment me not,</hi> that thou do not restrain me from doing mischief somewhere else; though I know I am <hi type="italic">sentenced,</hi> yet let me not be <hi type="italic">sent</hi> to the chains of darkness, or hindered from going to and fro, to <hi type="italic">devour.</hi>" <div eID="gen24496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24497" type="x-p"/> V. The account Christ took from this unclean spirit of his name. This we had not in Matthew. Christ asked him, <hi type="italic">What is thy name?</hi> Not but that Christ could call all the <hi type="italic">fallen</hi> stars, as well as the <hi type="italic">morning</hi> stars, by their names; but he demands this, that the standers by might be affected with the vast numbers and power of those malignant infernal spirits, as they had reason to be, when the answer was, <hi type="italic">My name is Legion, for we are many;</hi> a <hi type="italic">legion</hi> of soldiers among the Romans consisted, some say, of six thousand men, others of twelve thousand and five hundred; but the number of a legion with them, like that of a regiment with us, was not always the same. Now this intimates that the devils, the infernal powers, are, 1. <hi type="italic">Military</hi> powers; a legion is a number of soldiers in arms. The devils war against God and his glory, Christ and his gospel, men and their holiness and happiness. They are such as we are to <hi type="italic">resist</hi> and <hi type="italic">wrestle against,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Eph. vi. 12</reference>. 2. That they are <hi type="italic">numerous;</hi> he <hi type="italic">owns,</hi> or rather he <hi type="italic">boasts—We are many;</hi> as if he hoped to be <hi type="italic">too many</hi> for Christ himself to deal with. What multitudes of apostate spirits were there, and all enemies to God and man; when here were a legion posted to keep garrison in one poor wretched creature against Christ! Many there are that rise up against us. 3. That they are <hi type="italic">unanimous;</hi> they are <hi type="italic">many</hi> devils, and yet but <hi type="italic">one legion</hi> engaged in the same wicked cause; and therefore that cavil of the Pharisees, which supposed Satan to cast out Satan, and to be divided against himself, was altogether groundless. It was not <hi type="italic">one</hi> of this legion that betrayed the rest, for they all said, as one man, <hi type="italic">What have I to do with thee?</hi> 4. That they are very <hi type="italic">powerful;</hi> Who can stand before a <hi type="italic">legion?</hi> We are not a match for our spiritual enemies, in our own strength; but <hi type="italic">in the Lord, and in the power of his might,</hi> we shall be able to <hi type="italic">stand against them,</hi> though there are legions of them. 5. That there is <hi type="italic">order</hi> among them, as there is in a <hi type="italic">legion;</hi> there are <hi type="italic">principalities, and powers, and rulers of the darkness of this world,</hi> which supposes that there are those of a lower rank; the <hi type="italic">devil</hi> and his angels; the <hi type="italic">dragon</hi> and his; the prince of the devils and his subjects: which makes those enemies the more formidable. <div eID="gen24497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24498" type="x-p"/> VI. The request of this legion, that Christ would suffer them to go into a herd of swine that was <hi type="italic">feeding nigh unto the mountains</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.11">v. 11</reference>), those mountains which the demoniacs haunted, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.5">v. 5</reference>. Their request was, 1. That he <hi type="italic">would not send them away out of the country</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.10">v. 10</reference>); not only that he would not <hi type="italic">commit</hi> them, or <hi type="italic">confine</hi> them, to their infernal prison, and so <hi type="italic">torment them before the time;</hi> but that he would not <hi type="italic">banish</hi> them <hi type="italic">that country,</hi> as justly he might, because in this poor man they had been such a terror to it, and done so much mischief. They seem to have had a particular affection for <hi type="italic">that country;</hi> or, rather, a particular spite to it; and to have liberty to walk <hi type="italic">to and fro through</hi> the rest of <hi type="italic">the earth,</hi> will not serve (<reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job i. 7</reference>), unless the <hi type="italic">range of those mountains</hi> be allowed them for their pasture, <reference osisRef="Job.39.8">Job xxxix. 8</reference>. But why would they abide in <hi type="italic">that country?</hi> Grotius saith, Because in <hi type="italic">that country</hi> there were many <hi type="italic">apostate Jews,</hi> who had thrown themselves out of the covenant of God, and had thereby given Satan power over them. And some suggest, that, having by experience got the knowledge of the dispositions and manners of the people of that country, they could the more effectually do them mischief by their temptations. 2. That he would suffer them to <hi type="italic">enter into the swine,</hi> by destroying which they hoped to do more mischief to the souls of all the people in the country, than they could by entering into the body of any particular person, which therefore they did not ask leave to do, for they knew Christ would not grant it. <div eID="gen24498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24499" type="x-p"/> VII. The permission Christ gave them to enter into the swine, and the immediate destruction of the swine thereby; <hi type="italic">He gave them leave</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.13">v. 13</reference>), he did not forbid or restrain them, he let them do as they had a mind. Thus he would let the Gadarenes see what powerful spiteful enemies devils are, that they might thereby be induced to make him their Friend, who alone was able to control and conquer them, and had made it appear that he was so. Immediately the <hi type="italic">unclean spirits entered into the swine,</hi> which by the law were unclean creatures, and naturally love to <hi type="italic">wallow in the mire,</hi> the fittest place for them. Those that, like the swine, delight in <hi type="italic">the mire</hi> of sensual lusts, are fit habitations for Satan, and are, like Babylon, the <hi type="italic">hold of every foul spirit,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">cage of every unclean and hateful bird</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.18.2">Rev. xviii. 2</reference>), as pure souls are habitations of the Holy Spirit. The consequence of the devils entering into the swine, was, that they all <hi type="italic">ran mad</hi> presently, and ran headlong into the adjoining sea, where they were all drowned, to the number of <hi type="italic">two thousand.</hi> The man they possessed did only <hi type="italic">cut himself,</hi> for God had said, <hi type="italic">He is in your hands, only save his life.</hi> But thereby it appeared, that, if he had not been so restrained, the poor man would have <hi type="italic">drowned himself.</hi> See how much we are indebted to the providence of God, and the ministration of good angels, for our preservation from malignant spirits. <div eID="gen24499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24500" type="x-p"/> VIII. The report of all this dispersed through the country immediately. They that <hi type="italic">fed the swine,</hi> hastened to the owners, to give an account of their charge, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.14">v. 14</reference>. This drew the people together, to see what was done: and, 1. When they saw how wonderfully the poor man was cured, they hence conceived a <hi type="italic">veneration for Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.15">v. 15</reference>. They saw him that was <hi type="italic">possessed with the devil,</hi> and knew him well enough, by the same token that they had many a time been frightened at the sight of him; and were now as much surprised to see him <hi type="italic">sitting clothed and in his right mind;</hi> when Satan was cast out, he came to himself, and was his own man presently. Note, Those who are grave and sober, and live by rule and with consideration, thereby make it appear that by the power of Christ the devil's power is broken in their souls. The sight of this <hi type="italic">made them afraid;</hi> it astonished them, and forced them to own the power of Christ, and that he is <hi type="italic">worthy to be feared.</hi> But, 2. When they found that their swine were lost, they thence conceived a <hi type="italic">dislike of Christ,</hi> and wished to have rather his room than his company; they prayed him to <hi type="italic">depart out of their coasts,</hi> for they think not any good he can do them sufficient to make them amends for the loss of so many swine, fat swine, it may be, and ready for the market. Now the devils had what they would have; for by no handle do these evil spirits more effectually manage sinful souls than by that of the love of the world. They were afraid of some further punishment, if Christ should tarry among them, whereas, if they would but part with their sins, he had life and happiness for them; but, being loth to quit either their sins or their swine, they chose rather to abandon their Saviour. Thus <hi type="italic">they</hi> do, who, rather than let go a base lust, will throw away their interest in Christ, and their expectations from him. They should rather have argued, "If he has such a power as this over devils and all creatures, it is good having him our Friend; if the devils have leave to tarry <hi type="italic">in our country</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.10">v. 10</reference>), let us entreat <hi type="italic">him</hi> to tarry in it too, who alone can control them." But, instead of this, they wished him further off. Such strange misconstructions do carnal hearts make of the just judgments of God; instead of being by them driven to him as they ought, they set him at so much the greater distance; though he hath said, <hi type="italic">Provoke me not, and I will do you no hurt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.25.6">Jer. xxv. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen24500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24501" type="x-p"/> IX. An account of the conduct of the poor man after his deliverance. 1. He <hi type="italic">desired that he might go along with Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.18">v. 18</reference>), perhaps for fear lest the evil spirit should again seize him; or, rather, that he might receive instruction from him, being unwilling to stay among those heathenish people that desired him to depart. Those that are freed from the evil spirit, cannot but covet acquaintance and fellowship with Christ. 2. Christ <hi type="italic">would not suffer him</hi> to go with him, lest it should savour of ostentation, and to let him know that he could both protect and instruct him at a distance. And besides, he had other work for him to do; he must go home to his friends, and tell them what <hi type="italic">great things the Lord had done for him,</hi> the Lord Jesus had done; that Christ might be honoured, and his neighbours and friends might be edified, and invited to believe in Christ. He must take particular notice rather of Christ's <hi type="italic">pity</hi> than of his <hi type="italic">power,</hi> for that is it which especially he glories in; he must tell them what <hi type="italic">compassion</hi> the Lord had had on him in his misery. 3. The man, in a transport of joy, proclaimed, all the country over, what <hi type="italic">great things Jesus had done for him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.20">v. 20</reference>. This is a debt we owe both to Christ and to our brethren, that he may be glorified and they edified. And see what was the effect of it; <hi type="italic">All men did marvel,</hi> but few went any further. Many that cannot but wonder at the works of Christ, yet do not, as they ought, <hi type="italic">wonder after him.</hi>

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen24501" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Healing of the Bloody Issue.</title> <div sID="gen24502" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> And when Jesus was passed over again by ship unto the other side, much people gathered unto him: and he was nigh unto the sea. <hi type="super">22</hi> And, behold, there cometh one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name; and when he saw him, he fell at his feet, <hi type="super">23</hi> And besought him greatly, saying, My little daughter lieth at the point of death: <hi type="italic">I pray thee,</hi> come and lay thy hands on her, that she may be healed; and she shall live. 24 And <hi type="italic">Jesus</hi> went with him; and much people followed him, and thronged him. <hi type="super">25</hi> And a certain woman, which had an issue of blood twelve years, <hi type="super">26</hi> And had suffered many things of many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse, <hi type="super">27</hi> When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment. <hi type="super">28</hi> For she said, If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole. 29 And straightway the fountain of her blood was dried up; and she felt in <hi type="italic">her</hi> body that she was healed of that plague. 30 And Jesus, immediately knowing in himself that virtue had gone out of him, turned him about in the press, and said, Who touched my clothes? <hi type="super">31</hi> And his disciples said unto him, Thou seest the multitude thronging thee, and sayest thou, Who touched me? <hi type="super">32</hi> And he looked round about to see her that had done this thing. <hi type="super">33</hi> But the woman fearing and trembling, knowing what was done in her, came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth. <hi type="super">34</hi> And he said unto her, Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague. <div eID="gen24502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24503" type="x-p"/> The Gadarenes having desired Christ to leave their country, he did not stay to trouble them long, but presently went by water, as he came, back <hi type="italic">to the other side</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.21">v. 21</reference>), and there <hi type="italic">much people gathered to him.</hi> Note, If there be some that reject Christ, yet there are others that receive him, and bid him welcome. A despised gospel will <hi type="italic">cross the water,</hi> and go where it will have better entertainment. Now among the many that applied themselves to him, <div eID="gen24503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24504" type="x-p"/> I. Here is one, that comes <hi type="italic">openly</hi> to <hi type="italic">beg</hi> a cure for a sick child; and it is no less a person than one of the <hi type="italic">rulers of the synagogue,</hi> one that presided in the synagogue-worship or, as some think, one of the judges of the consistory court, which was in every city, consisting of <hi type="italic">twenty-three.</hi> He was not named in Matthew, he is here, <hi type="italic">Jairus,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Jair,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.10.3">Judg. x. 3</reference>. He addressed himself to Christ, though a ruler, with great humility and reverence; <hi type="italic">When he saw him, he fell at his feet,</hi> giving honour to him as one really greater than he appeared to be; and with great importunity, he <hi type="italic">besought him greatly,</hi> as one in earnest, as one that not only valued the mercy he came for, but that knew he could obtain it no where else. The case is this, He has a <hi type="italic">little daughter,</hi> about twelve years old, the darling of the family, and she <hi type="italic">lies a dying;</hi> but he believes that if Christ will but come, and <hi type="italic">lay his hands upon her,</hi> she will return even from the gates of the grave. entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen24509" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Daughter of Jairus Restored to Life.</title> <div sID="gen24510" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> While he yet spake, there came from the ruler of the synagogue's <hi type="italic">house certain</hi> which said, Thy daughter is dead: why troublest thou the Master any further? <hi type="super">36</hi> As soon as Jesus heard the word that was spoken, he saith unto the ruler of the synagogue, Be not afraid, only believe. <hi type="super">37</hi> And he suffered no man to follow him, save Peter, and James, and John the brother of <reference osisRef="Jas.38">James. 38</reference> And he cometh to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and seeth the tumult, and them that wept and wailed greatly. <hi type="super">39</hi> And when he was come in, he saith unto them, Why make ye this ado, and weep? the damsel is not dead, but sleepeth. <hi type="super">40</hi> And they laughed him to scorn. But when he had put them all out, he taketh the father and the mother of the damsel, and them that were with him, and entereth in where the damsel was lying. <hi type="super">41</hi> And he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise. <hi type="super">42</hi> And straightway the damsel arose, and walked; for she was <hi type="italic">of the age</hi> of twelve years. And they were astonished with a great astonishment. <hi type="super">43</hi> And he charged them straitly that no man should know it; and commanded that something should be given her to eat. <div eID="gen24510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24511" type="x-p"/> Diseases and deaths came into the world by the sin and disobedience of the first Adam; but by the grace of the second Adam both are conquered. Christ, having healed an incurable disease, here goes on to triumph over death, as in the beginning of the chapter he had triumphed over an outrageous devil. <div eID="gen24511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24512" type="x-p"/> I. The melancholy news is brought to Jairus, that his <hi type="italic">daughter is dead,</hi> and therefore, if Christ be as other physicians, he comes too late. While there is life, there is hope, and room for the use of means; but when life is gone, it is past recall; <hi type="italic">Why troublest thou the Master any further?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.35">v. 35</reference>. Ordinarily, the proper thought in this case, is, "The matter is determined, the will of God is done, and I submit, I acquiesce; <hi type="italic">The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away. entries.content_plain: The Daughter of Jairus Restored to Life. 35 While he yet spake, there came from the ruler of the synagogue's house certain which said, Thy daughter is dead: why troublest thou the Master any further? 36 As soon as Jesus heard the word that was spoken, he saith unto the ruler of the synagogue, Be not afraid, only believe. 37 And he suffered no man to follow him, save Peter, and James, and John the brother of James. 38 And he cometh to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and seeth the tumult, and them that wept and wailed greatly. 39 And when he was come in, he saith unto them, Why make ye this ado, and weep? the damsel is not dead, but sleepeth. 40 And they laughed him to scorn. And they were astonished with a great astonishment. 43 And he charged them straitly that no man should know it; and commanded that something should be given her to eat. Christ, having healed an incurable disease, here goes on to triumph over death, as in the beginning of the chapter he had triumphed over an outrageous devil. I. The melancholy news is brought to Jairus, that his daughter is dead, and therefore, if Christ be as other physicians, he comes too late. While there is life, there is hope, and room for the use of means; but when life is gone, it is past recall; Why troublest thou the Master any further? v. 35 . Ordinarily, the proper thought in this case, is, "The matter is determined, the will of God is done, and I submit, I acquiesce; The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away. Christ therefore soon determines this matter; " Be not afraid that my coming will be to no purpose, only believe that I will make it turn to a good account." Note, 1. That it was evident beyond dispute, that the child was really and truly dead. Christ's healing the woman with the bloody issue, in the way as he was going to raise Jairus's daughter to life, ver. 21-43 . These three miracles we had the story of before ( Matt. viii. 28, and Matt. ix. 18 , and c.) but more fully related here.
